utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-54-R77.5, in the case against Florence Hartmann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to confirm, Mrs. Hartmann, that you are receiving interpretation and can understand the proceedings. Did you hear me, Madam Hartmann?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you hear the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Should you encounter any difficulties in this regard at any time, please let me know. Okay. Could we have the appearances for the day starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My name is Bruce MacFarlane. I'm an attorney from Canada appearing as amicus curiae Prosecutor in these proceedings. Along with me is Lori Ann Wanlin, also from Canada.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: If it please, Your Honour, good afternoon. My name is Karim Khan, and I appear together with my co-counsel Guenal Mettraux, to my left. To my right is our legal assistant, Arina Koligina. And to her right is our legal intern, Samira Mohammed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. I'm not suggesting anything might arise, but should anything confidentially arise during the proceedings, I hope your intern and legal assistant will be aware of their obligations in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, they are of course, and they have as are required of all legal assistants and interns signed confidentiality agreements and are bound by the respective code of conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may just deal with the procedural background. This is the second Status Conference in this case. The previous Status Conference was held on the 30th of January 2009 prior to trial which had been scheduled for the 5th and 6th of February, 2009. Since that time an issue of disqualification of two Judges of the Chamber arose and has been decided. We are now -- we now have a new bench composed and already -- and ready for trial proceedings to continue. Pursuant to Rule 65 bis (A) of the rules, the purpose of a status conference is to one, organise exchanges between the parties so as to ensure an expeditious preparation for trial; and two, to review the status of this case and to allow the accused to raise issues, including issues related to the accused's mental and physical condition. Mr. Khan, I know that the accused is not in pre-trial detention, but I still have to ask you the question. Are you aware of any issue related to her mental and physical condition that needs to be disclosed to the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. I'm most grateful for the invitation, but there's nothing that pertains to those matters raised by Your Honour just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And the senior legal officer sent a draft agenda to the parties and invited items from the parties. We will follow the order of out items in that agenda. And the agenda is -- the items are as follows: The review of recently decided motions; review of still pending motions, or decisions, rather; status of disclosure; status of agreed facts; administrative matters; calendar for future proceedings; and items proposed by the parties. Let me start with the recently decided motions. The following decisions were recently issued, including four decisions today. There was a decision on Prosecution motion to amend the Rule 65 ter list filed on the 4th of May, 2009; decision on Defence motion for binding order to the Registry filed confidentially on the 6th of May, 2009; decision on requests pursuant to Rule 74, filed on the 6th of May, 2009; decision on motion for certification to appeal Trial Chamber's decision regarding stay of proceedings for abuse of process issued on the 13th of May, 2009; decision on motion for certification to appeal Trial Chamber's decision on Defence motion for reconsideration, dated the 14th of January, 2009, issued on the 13th of May, 2009; decision on Defence motion for leave to appeal Trial Chamber's decision regarding Prosecution witness statements filed on the 19th of May, 2009; decision on Defence motion for certification to appeal; decision on motion for issuance of subpoena to amicus curiae Prosecutor, filed on the 19th of May, 2009; decision on Defence motion pertaining to the nullification of Trial Chamber's orders and decisions filed on the 19th of May, 2009; and finally decision on Prosecution motion for admission of evidence from the bar table pursuant to Rule 89(C), filed on the 19th of May, 2009. Have I missed out any decision that's outstanding according to the parties? I am aware, Mr. MacFarlane, that there is a decision outstanding on the motion, Prosecution motion, to expedite the trial. In the view of the Chamber, these proceedings this afternoon and as we will see later in the agenda, that decision will be rendered moot. And it is not the intention of the Chamber, therefore, to issue a decision on that one. Thank you. Okay. May we then move on to the status of disclosure. Are there any remaining disclosure obligations under the rules which need to be fulfilled, Mr. MacFarlane?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. On my review of the rules and the material that's been provided, it's my assessment that disclosure has been provided. My learned friend and I have had some correspondence on other matters. He's requested some matters, and I've responded, and there's areas that are in dispute, but from my perspective disclosure has been provided in accordance with the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: As mentioned by the amicus Prosecutor there is one outstanding matter. The Prosecutor last week, in the course of last week has indicated that he would respond positively to a request made by the Defence in relation to the disclosure of some material and information that we've sought. This is the only outstanding matter in our belief that remains to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So it can be recorded that this will be finalised very quickly, because there's agreement between the parties at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We would hope so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Then if there isn't anything else on that, we will move on to the status of agreed facts. In the Prosecution's statement of admissions of the parties and matters not in dispute dated the 6th of February, 2009, it is indicated that there may be more agreed facts before trial. Subsequently, on the 9th of February, 2009, the Defence filed what was entitled a motion pursuant to Rule 65 ter which set forth additional facts in an annex which the parties purportedly agreed were not in dispute. Just to clarify, is this -- is it the position of the parties that the facts set forth in these two filings are agreed between the parties and to be considered as evidence by the Trial Chamber? You want to take the first part of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for one clarification for the record. It's quite correct that the first filing put forward by my friend the amicus Prosecutor is dated the 6th of February. The Defence motion where further agreed facts were set out is, I believe, dated the 7th of February, and those facts are agreed as far as the Defence are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: It's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The date 9th of February here, I think refers to the filing date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that may be -- that may be so. [Overlapping speakers] ... check that. But the document itself is dated on its face the 7th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Khan. And are there no further developments with regard to agreed facts? Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: First of all I should say I agree with my learned friend in terms of the status of agreed statement of facts, but to my knowledge, there are no further areas of agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: That's the extent of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the extent of it. Thank you so much. Let's move to what is entitled administrative matters. The Chamber is not in possession of an English translation of the Flammarion contract admitted by the recent decision of the Chamber on the bar table motion by the Prosecutor. Do you want to say something on that, Mr. MacFarlane?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Translation is in process as we speak, and I expect will be completed as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then you -- I guess I need not say anything further about that. As soon as possible. How -- how soon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the requested date for the translation was the 29th of this month, but if we receive direction from the Chamber, we will arrange to have that date changed and brought forward if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I understand it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Given the schedule of the people who are doing the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: My understanding is it is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it is possible, can we bring it as forward as -- is possibly --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: We will communicate that as soon as we're finished here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour there are two short issues pertaining to the translation. The first one pertains to the transcript of a CD which Your Honours have admitted by a decision of this morning. And the query that we have is whether or not the Prosecutor intends to submit the transcript to CLSS with a view to ensure the accuracy of the record. We've indicated in our response to their application some concern about the accuracy and completeness of the record and transcript that was made of this conversation, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we take a step back before you go to the accuracy. Do we know who translated that? Was it not translate by CLSS?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we understand from the face of the record that there were complaints made in particular by our client and her then-counsel as to the quality of the interpretation that was given to her words. What we wonder is whether the Prosecutor would be good enough to indicate first who, in fact, did the translation, and secondly, whether the matter has been submitted to CLSS for the purpose of accurate translation. The completeness, Your Honour, is also an issue that we would wish to raise to the extent that some of the word heard or pronounced during the interview have not been re-transcript [sic] on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now let me be sure I understand what you are saying. The interview was recorded somewhere electronically, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After the recording, whatever language it was recorded in, it was also transcribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what has been filed this morning is the transcript that comes out of the recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's correct again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And when did your client complain about the accuracy of that transcription?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It was made at the time, Your Honour, during the interview. During -- in several parts of the transcript there are complaints about the inaccuracy of her words as communicated to the Prosecutor. Therefore, the translation, as far as the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the words of your client will have been recorded directly in the electronic machine at the time of speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, our concern, Your Honour, is precisely this: That the transcript which is in English does not accurately reflect the content of the CD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but -- what I -- sir, has your client -- I'm trying to understand how your client during the interview could complain about a transcription that was to be made subsequent to the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, if I wasn't clear. She wasn't complaining about the transcription at the time. What she was complaining about is the quality of the translation that was being made. The translation, perhaps, and I should give that background information, was not made by an independent interpreter or qualified interpreter, as we understand. It was being done by an assistant or a colleague of Mr. MacFarlane. And in the course of that interview she complained about the poor quality of the translation that was made of her word. And our concern, Your Honour, is that this poor translation is reflected into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But what I'm saying is what your client said during the interview, her own words were recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: The French, as we understand, Your Honour, is not recorded. What we understand was recorded was the translation that was made of what was believed to be said by her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Am I to understand that during the recording of the interview there was a start, stop, start, stop? When she spoke in French, they switched off, and then when somebody translated, they switched on?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We believe that as far as the mechanism are concerned, only the Prosecutor could clarify this matter. We understand that the recording was continual, but that's only the English was translated, that is, the English of Mr. MacFarlane and the English of the interpreter. And I would stand corrected if that's inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane -- or before I go to Mr. MacFarlane. I am trying to make a distinction here between any interpretation to your client during the interview if she needed an interpreter at all and the recording of the interview itself and then the subsequent translation and transcription of the recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: What we understand, Your Honour, is that the transcription is, or should be, at least, a correct transcription of what was said in English. Our concern is whether the translation that was made at the time of the interview accurately portrays the content of what would our client was saying. And to the extent that it can be determined from the CD and from her complaint, we wonder whether it would be a good idea to ensure the accuracy of what was said to transmit it to CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, do you have any response to what your colleague is saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: With the greatest of respect to my learned friend, I think that there's some confusion that's crept into his filings and his submission today. And I recognise the fact that my learned friend wasn't there at the time, so I'm taking that into account. What happened was this: At the time of the interview which took place in the accused's counsel boardroom, it was agreed that I would pose questions to the accused in English, she would respond in French. And I had the benefit of an interpreter, not a translator but an interpreter, in essence whispering in my ear so that I understood fully. I have a capacity in French but not a full capacity, so I could understand the nature of the response. That was not -- that was simply for my assistance in the process. It was never intended to form part of the evidentiary record at all. It was not part of the evidence that we're tendering. That was simply to assist me in the back and forth between the accused and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In what language did the accused speak to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: The accused spoke in French. I supposed questions in English. And she indicated that she understood the questions that were being posed in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if you say the accused spoke to you in French, did she have any interpretation of what you were saying in English into French?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: No. She indicated that she didn't need that. Then if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The roles were reversed here. She didn't need an interpreter. You needed an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the interpreter was whispering into your ear. She was not telling everybody --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, can we sit in one court --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: If I may just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Hartmann. Sorry, just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you do want to chat to your counsel, Madam Hartmann, do so quietly, please. Thank you. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. It was intended for my benefit, it may well be that others in the room heard portions of it. That's entirely possible, but in terms of the purpose of the interpretation, it was solely for my benefit so that I would understand in more detail the nature of the answer that was being provided. I -- I have, as I said before, I had a capacity to understand, but I wanted to make sure that I understood better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me find this out. If Madam Hartmann spoke in French and you spoke in English, was her French response recorded?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes, it was. My question in English and her response in French were both fully recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. And what happened to the recording? Was there -- was the recording then submitted somewhere for translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And where was it submitted to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: It was submitted to the Tribunal. It's my understanding it was CLSS that did the translation. I think what my learned friend is referring to is that some -- so that the exchange -- my English posing of the question is -- is transcribed in English. Madam Hartmann's response to my questions was translated into English. On occasion in the transcript the CLSS appears to have included some of what I'll refer to as the whisperings to me. I think that's what my learned friend is referring to. On -- often it will say unintelligible or a portion, but those were the whisperings to me to assist me. That's not -- I'm not tendering that. That's not part of the evidence. What is the evidence is the transcription of the exchange between the accused and I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. MacFarlane. Mr. Mettraux? Mr. Khan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, forgive me. Perhaps I can try to assist, at least to the best of my limited abilities. Your Honour, the nub of the issue is, and what my learned friend fails to grasp in my respectful submission, is that acting at that stage as the amicus investigator, it is inappropriate for him to make a unilateral assessment as to my client's ability and facility in the English language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, under Article 21, there are minimum rights. Now, Your Honour, the difficulty is this, that whilst the transcript does detail purportedly the question in English and the reply of my client in English, the original in French, which is on the tape or on the electronic recording device, is not detailed, and we are not certain and it does not appear from the best of our ability that has been accurately or properly or independently translated. Rather, the converse is true, that the translator selected by the Prosecutor, not certified, to the best of our knowledge, not independent, has taken it upon herself to whisper in the ear of the amicus Prosecutor and those utterances, those mutterings and whisperings and also those purported translations are recorded in the transcript. And it is rather a muddled state of affairs, and this is what my learned friend himself concedes at the moment. So, Your Honour, all we're asking for, this ambiguity can easily be remedied. This confusion can be easily be easily obliterated by submitting the original electronic recording device to the court interpretation service and asking them to translate from the French, I'm sorry to say it, from the horse's mouth, from the French directly to the English, and then of course just transcribe what my learned friend says in English. And that way we would have a completely accurate record without any -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is what he says has been done except in their diligence they translated even the whisperings. But I've just been told now before you stood up that the translation and the transcription was done by CLSS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if my learned friend's undertaking to the Court is that what is transcribed is not the translation of his interpreter but is the actual words of my client, then of course I'm willing to accept his undertaking in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is what's just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if that's the case, I will accept counsel's undertaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then another point I wanted to raise with respect to the issues that those very filings related to those recordings, at this stage I personally have not sort of gone through them yet, but Mr. MacFarlane, you might perhaps be able to guide us here. There may or may not be confidential utterances in -- in those transcriptions, and it would be helpful if sometime, at the appropriate time, before the trial begins, you can indicate -- maybe both the parties can indicate which of the documents should be public and which confidential. At this stage, I guess we'll ask Registry to keep them confidential until such time as you have given advice on which are public. Okay. That disposes of that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one related matter. The other issue which would be of huge assistance is my learned friend has indicated that there are aspects of that transcript that he realise upon and aspects that he does not rely upon. It would be useful for the Defence to be on notice as to those exact parts. And I would ask that an order be given that he delete, it can be even with a pen, he should delete those portions of the transcript which he says he is not relying upon so we don't need to concern ourselves with those portions. I think that's only fair as a matter of case management.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I heard him to say that the whisperings into his ear. So I would imagine that what then should be of importance to the parties is where your client is speaking and where Mr. MacFarlane is speaking. Where anybody else is speaking other than your client's counsel, if she had counsel at the time, if there's any fourth person around, that person must be deleted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's quite right. But all I'm asking is that the person that's prosecuting my client clean up the record so I don't have to muse what are whisperings and what is evidence. And it's not an onerous task; it's a task that would happen in any court anywhere in the world, that those portions of the interview that he's not relying upon to prove his case should be either marked, identified, or redacted. Your Honour, it's a very simple task, and it's one that would not put over -- would not compel my learned friend to overly exert himself. And I would ask formally for an order in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think that that actually would be helpful to everyone. I'm quite prepared to go through on a line-by-line basis and excise those areas that I referred to as whisperings. That's probably not a totally accurate description, but those portions that were interpretations simply for my benefit that are not part of the evidentiary record and which I'm not tendering. So I'm quite happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it is possible to delete them or redact them somehow, it would be helpful. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, related to that, it's a side issue to an issue Your Honour mentioned earlier is the Flammarion contract. Your Honour of course has asked that that be translated. But again, just as a matter of case management, it would be of assistance to me if my learned friend can go through and highlight what portion of that contract he's relying upon, because of course we've read the pre-trial brief of my learned friend, but it's not clear to me the basis upon which he is adducing that contract and the purpose for which it's being tendered. So it may be that one portion is a matter of dispute or controversy or could otherwise be agreed. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think -- I think that's a matter to be raise at trial, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAHN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, so be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... at trial, what portion of the contract he is relying on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At this point, it's a question of disclosure. He's disclosed to you the contract that he's going to rely on, and he will tell you when he gets to trial what portion of it he is going to rely on, if he's relying on a portion only. I don't know whether he's relying on a portion only or on the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I take the point with the greatest of respect, but it does go down to proper notice. It's not clear to me the relevance of this document, and it's not -- it's not touched upon in the pre-trial brief either. And ordinarily the pre-trial brief together with the supporting documents is to alert counsel as to the facts in issue and the focus of the Prosecutor's case. Given that I have not a -- the merest idea as to the relevance of the contract itself, I am asking either that he go through and point out the portions of the contract that are relevant or at least maybe a 30 second spiel, elaborate the purpose for which he is tendering the document so that I can properly prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But has he told you the purpose for which he is tendering any other document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, ordinarily according to the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, the pre-trial brief can be taken in conjunction with the documents that are disclosed, 65 ter documents and the like, to put parties on proper notice. One doesn't simply bring a wheelbarrow in of documents and say somehow it's tangentially relevant. I would ask for some specificity in that regard, and it needn't -- I'm quite content for my learned friend to stand up now and just illuminate me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think that perhaps what my learned friend should do is check his earlier e-mails because we did have an exchange back and forth on this, and I outlined the reason for which the evidence is being tendered. So he already has that in his possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. MacFarlane. Okay. Let me just say by way of caution and by way of indication of how we run the trial in this court, sir, counsel is very welcome to either prosecute or defend his counsel's case as vociferously as one can, but I think we should stay within the realms of courtesy. You're talking here of one document. I don't know how thick the document is, could hardly be referred to as a wheelbarrow of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept with due humility the admonition, but perhaps the frustration is caused by issues that we have raised, that we haven't benefitted from statements in this case. That is the context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are all frustrated, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are all -- our nerves or all on edge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But nonetheless we stay within the bounds of courtesy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's not a wheelbarrow, it's certainly a suitcase, because I have three files in front of me, and that's only a portion of the documents and filings in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm talking of the document that you say is tangentially relevant, maybe tangentially relevant. I'm talking about the contact. I don't know anything about it. I don't know how thick this document is. But we're talking about one document here; we're not talking about the entire disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I will move on. And I take admonition on board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Shall we then go to the calendar for future proceedings. On the 8th of January, 2009, the amicus Prosecutor filed his pre-trial brief in this case, and on the 15th of January, 2009, the Defence filed its pre-trial brief in the case. No additional procedural requirements stand in the way for scheduling the case for trial. The Chamber is therefore scheduling the case for trial in the week of 8th to the 12th of June 2009. Scheduling Order will follow, but first I would like to hear the parties' views on how much time you consider to be necessary for the presentation of your cases. And I know that this has been given previously. The Prosecution had requested six hours, and the Defence requested 13 hours, but that included three hours to call the Prosecutor as a witness. I'm not quite sure what the position is, and I think there is also a witness that the Prosecution has dropped. Okay. Are you able to start, Mr. MacFarlane?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: In terms of the case per se excluding argument and other things, the case per se.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The hearing of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The hearing of evidence, the calling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... Yes, the hearing of evidence. That would include the tendering of the documentary evidence and viva voce evidence. My best assessment is four or five hours. Probably four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Khan? Are you done?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We'd seek leave from the Chamber if it is feasible perhaps to give a -- a clear undertaking later today if that is acceptable to the Chamber. There maybe some scheduling issues for one of the counsel in this case, and we would like to, with the leave of the Chamber and with the kindness in this case of the Chamber, if we could be given a couple of hours after the hearing to go through this matter and try to facilitate it. As far as the length of the Defence case is concerned, Your Honour has indicated the position and the request of the Defence. We believe it is a reasonable amount of time for the evidence which we propose to present to the Chamber. We would also like to seek an indication, perhaps not as to the time, but a general idea as to the time allotted to each party for closing argument which would be of assistance to the Defence in terms of preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux, I'm not quite sure what your position is. You start off by saying you would like to give an undertaking today if it's acceptable to the Chamber, but then you go on to say that the Chamber has indicated the position that the Defence had requested, and you believe that that is a reasonable amount of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, do you want to tell us later what time you're going to use, or are you saying the time you gave us last time you stand by?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We do stand by, Your Honour, as to the time. The issue that we have is one of the dates, the 8th to the 12th of June. And with leave of the Chamber, we would respectfully ask that this matter be considered further by the Defence. As indicated, there is a conflict of schedule for one of the counsel at least, and we would wish to organise and ensure that this is not the case so that we can indicate to the Chamber later today that we don't have a clash of schedule. As far as the time necessary for the Defence, we stick to our previous position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's talk about the scheduling. As you sit there, are you saying, sir -- as you sit there and stand there are you saying, sir, that the period 8th to the 12th would not be suitable to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. What we would wish to do, however, is to ensure that this is feasible. And this is what we would wish to undertake in the later part of the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. When you do advise the Chamber later this afternoon, can you also copy the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. And a final decision of the Chamber on the number of witnesses and length of the Prosecution case will be formally rendered at the Pre-Trial Conference on the first day of trial, okay. Now, items proposed by the parties. The parties, as I indicated -- were to indicate by close of business yesterday whether they wished to propose any items for consideration at the status conference. The Defence this morning after the deadline proposed the following items they might wish to raise. I'm not sure whether they are going to raise them or have you decided to -- not to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, thank you very much. Most of them have now been dealt with by Your Honour, so there's no need to go further into those. There are two issues, however, that we would wish to bring to the further attention of the Chamber. The first one pertains to the Rule 65 ter list of the Defence. At this stage there's a number of documents that we're going through and which we may wish to add to our Rule 65 ter list. We will give a list this afternoon of those proposed documents to the Prosecutor so that he can review them, review the list in question. There is also the possibility, Your Honour, of a supplementary or an application for an amendment to the Rule 65 ter list of witnesses. We are now considering the possibility of two additional witnesses. We also are considering the possibility of having those witnesses 92 bis'd with a view to expedite matter. This will be done as soon as possible and as soon as practical. The second issue, Your Honour, is related to the one that I have just mentioned, and it is the fact that the Defence is still seeking to conduct limited investigation which could lead to one of these witnesses being proposed as an additional witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. MacFarlane, I know you didn't respond. You don't have anything you want to add to the agenda?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I did not respond because until the end of yesterday, I didn't have any additional issues. But there is one issue that I would like to raise arising from one of the decisions this morning, if I might address the Chamber on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: In the decision concerning the issue of a subpoena on the amicus, there's a footnote. I believe it's footnote 25 which, along with the accompanying text, refers to potential reference of posing questions to the Prosecutor with a view to eliciting answers. And the issue I'd like to raise is in order to ensure that we have an orderly process and a meaningful process, it seems to me that two things need to be addressed, perhaps by way of guidelines so that we know how this could unfold if my learned friend intends to use that suggestion. Guidelines would be helpful for both counsel, I expect, and my -- my overarching suggestion is that the Chamber control and manage the process, as opposed to it being a counsel process, which would include at least two elements. First of all, the questions, if they are to be posed, be posed well in advance of the trial so there's an opportunity to review documents and obtain documents if that's necessary in order to respond accurately. It would not, in my respectful submission, be helpful to pose the questions on the day of the trial or in the middle of a trial. I think that they should be developed and posed in advance so that we can have an orderly process. And secondly -- so that's an issue of timing. Secondly, I respectfully submit that there ought to be a review by the Chamber of the appropriateness of the question that's being posed to ensure that it is a proper question, that it is focussed, that it's not intended to elicit information which is not properly receivable, and so on. So I'm suggesting firstly, a timing issue; and secondly, a review issue on the part of the Chamber. The questions that my learned friend has been posing to me in the past several weeks, if not several months, have been extremely broad and almost incapable of answering. They -- perhaps for the record I could outline one of the most recent questions that was received to give the Chamber a flavour of the -- of the types of questions that could be posed, and I have no reason to believe that they won't be along these lines. On May 1st, which is only two and a half weeks ago this question was posed subsequent to my providing some documents to my learned friend. So documents were provided; this is a follow-up. And the question was this: In addition to the records of contacts/communications that you have already disclosed to us, there have -- has there been other contacts in whatever form between yourself or your staff and representatives of the Chamber or Registry as regard the conduct of your investigation or prosecution of the case, including the manner thereof, the course or focus of your investigation, the nature of your findings, and any other matter pertaining to the carrying out of your mandate as investigator and/or Prosecutor that took place and for which your record has not yet been disclosed to the Defence? As the Chamber can appreciate, that's an incredibly broad question. Could well be characterized as a fishing expedition. But it's become even worse in the past week or so because my learned friend recently wrote to me and said, In addition to the documents that you're seeking, it would be helpful if you could give us recollections of contacts with all of these people, if there were any. So my point is that there needs to be a Chamber review of the appropriateness to ensure that Rule 70(A) is not being violated and other principles embraced by the Tribunal are not being violated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you want to respond to that, Mr. Mettraux?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, since the matter is still pending with the Prosecution. We would simply indicate as a response that the problem we're encountering, Your Honour, is in a traditional form the Defence would have an opportunity to examine or cross-examine the person competent and responsible for the investigation. In this case we find ourself in the difficult position and understand the difficult position of our colleague as well of having to be that person. What we would specify, however, in relation to the breadth, Your Honour, is, yes, our colleague has mentioned one e-mail. However, it is to be read in the context of many search e-mails that we've sent and that specified what we were looking for and what we were after. Furthermore, as indicated, the Prosecutor has accepted now to provide us with the material that we seeking and which is very clear on its substance. I don't wish to say more, Your Honour, at this stage. As indicated, the Prosecution has now accepted to give us the information that he is complaining about. I would just add this, Your Honour. In relation to the suggestion that we made to the Prosecutor that he should provide us with his recollection of those meetings. The reason for this, Your Honour, was the Prosecutor indicated to us that he was unable to provide us with the actual records of those meetings which he said were in another country. The solution that we found to expedite matter was to ask him to provide us at this stage and pending his delivery of the material with his recollection. It was simply a practical solution to expedite matter. We were not asking for something extraordinary but searching for a way to facilitate things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. I think the Chamber has noted what the parties have said on the point, and we'll look into the matter. Thank you so much. Was that all you had, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. It does seem as if there is nothing else. Nothing from the Chamber's side, nothing from the Defence side. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just perhaps just one matter, with your leave, that wasn't touched upon. My learned friend has asked that in the event that we're granted leave to call -- call him as a witness, advance notice be given of questions. Your Honour, of course that's a matter for your discretion in due course, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But are we talking about the same thing? I thought he was talking about him being asked questions not being called as a witness. You're talking about being called as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if we are asking questions, of course we've had communication, and we are getting a response from my learned friend. Of course, we say rather late in the day. But if there is a nonresponse, we are quite content to make application and file it with the Trial Chamber for the appropriate relief. So it needn't concern Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's not -- [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... overly much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If we're talking about calling the amicus curiae as a witness, we talk about that. If we talk about asking him questions, we talk about asking him questions. I don't think we should mix the two in one. He was responding to the issue of a footnote to a decision which refers to him being asked questions, and I do not -- I have no special recollection of that footnote, but what I am saying is the issue he's raising is being asked questions not being called as a witness, and these are two different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am grateful. But when one asks questions to the opposing party, it's completely at large. The Prosecution can ask any question of us, and we can ask any question that we deem appropriate to the Prosecutor. Now, of course the response is not a matter of compulsion; it's a matter of volition. And if either party, whether it be the Prosecutor or the Defence, feel aggrieved there are appropriate remedies. So in any event, the order requested is unnecessary, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. It looks like that brings us to the conclusion, unless somebody you -- you are looking at me, Mr. MacFarlane, as if you have a last word to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Only for the purposes of being absolutely clear. And I'm not sure if my learned friend has had an opportunity to read the decisions and consider the decisions from this morning. But just for the sake of the record and to be absolutely clear, what I was referring to was the decision rendered today, the 19th of May, with respect to the issuance of a subpoena to an amicus curiae Prosecutor. And I'm referring in particular to paragraph 7 and 8 and footnote 25. That's all that I'm referring to. I'm not talking about the issue of being called as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Your Honour, I hadn't seen that decision. It hasn't arrived in my in-box.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Then that brings us to the end the Status Conference, and the conference stands adjourned. Court adjourned.
